```{r}
#| warning: false
# Set seed
set.seed(13)

# Plot A
h_1 <- function(x){
  x
}
h_2 <- function(x){
  x / 2
}
curve(expr = h_1,
      from = 0,
      to = 12,
      xlab = "t",
      ylab = "h(t)",
      main = "Plot A")
curve(expr = h_2,
      add = TRUE,
      lty = 2)
grid()

# Plot B
cll_1 <- function(x){
  log(x)
}
cll_2 <- function(x){
  log(x) / 2 - 1
}
curve(expr = cll_1,
      from = 0,
      to = 12,
      xlab = "t",
      ylab = "log(-log(S(t)))",
      main = "Plot B")
curve(expr = cll_2,
      add = TRUE,
      lty = 2)
grid()

# Plot C
S_1 <- function(x){
  exp(-(x / 5)^2)
}
S_2 <- function(x){
  1 - x / 12
}
curve(expr = S_1,
      from = 0,
      to = 12,
      xlab = "t",
      ylab = "S(t)",
      main = "Plot C")
curve(expr = S_2,
      add = TRUE,
      lty = 2)
grid()

# Plot D
h_3 <- function(x){
  sin(x / 8 * 2 * pi) + 1
}
h_4 <- function(x){
  h_3(x) / 2
}
curve(expr = h_3,
      from = 0,
      to = 12,
      xlab = "t",
      ylab = "h(t)",
      main = "Plot D")
curve(expr = h_4,
      add = TRUE,
      lty = 2)
grid()

# Plot E
h_5 <- function(x){
  x + 2
}
h_6 <- function(x){
  x + 4
}
curve(expr = h_5,
      from = 0,
      to = 12,
      xlab = "t",
      ylab = "h(t)",
      main = "Plot E")
curve(expr = h_6,
      add = TRUE,
      lty = 2)
grid()

# Plot F
cll_3 <- function(x){
  2 * log(x) - 2 * log(2)
}
cll_4 <- function(x){
  2 * log(x) - 2 * log(2) - 1
}
curve(expr = cll_3,
      from = 2,
      to = 12,
      xlab = "t",
      ylab = "log(-log(S(t)))",
      main = "Plot F",
      ylim = c(cll_4(2),
               cll_3(12)))
curve(expr = cll_4,
      add = TRUE,
      lty = 2)
grid()
```



## Problem 1

Each of the plots above shows two curves,
one for each group in a randomized controlled trial.
For each plot,
identify whether the proportional hazards assumption is met.
Each is worth one point.

### Part (a)


 Plot A


(i) Proportional hazards assumption is met.
(ii) Proportional hazards assumption is not met.


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

i

The solid hazard function is twice the dashed hazard function.

:::
        
### Part (b)

Plot B

(i) Proportional hazards assumption is met.
(ii) Proportional hazards assumption is not met.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

ii

The complementary log-log functions are not parallel.

:::
        
### Part (c)

Plot C

(i) Proportional hazards assumption is met.
(ii) Proportional hazards assumption is not met.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

ii

The survival curves cross, so the hazards can't be proportional.

:::
        
### Part (d)

Plot D

(i) Proportional hazards assumption is met.
(ii) Proportional hazards assumption is not met.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

i

The solid hazard function is twice the dashed hazard function.

:::
        
### Part (e)

Plot E

(i) Proportional hazards assumption is met.
(ii) Proportional hazards assumption is not met.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

ii

The hazard functions are parallel, but they need to be proportional.

:::

### Part (f)

Plot F

(i) Proportional hazards assumption is met.
(ii) Proportional hazards assumption is not met.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

i

The complementary log-log functions are parallel.

:::

## Problem 2

For each of the following examples,
identify the best analysis method from the options provided.
Each is worth one point.

### Part (a)


You want to know whether using mechanical lifts decreases the incidence of musculoskeletal
injuries among nurses in hospitals.
You randomly assign some hospitals to receive mechanical lifts;
those that don't receive the lifts serve as controls.
You measure a variety of variables for each hospital,
including the number of nurses employed,
how many hours they work,
how many patients are treated,
what they are treated for, etc.
Your primary outcome measure is the number of new musculoskeletal injuries
in the six months following installation of the lifts.


(i) Cox regression
(ii) Logistic regression
(iii) Multinomial regression (baseline category logit model)
(iv) Poisson regression


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

iv

The outcome is a count, so Poisson regression is the best bet.

:::

### Part (b)


You want to know the impact of journaling on mental health.
You recruit undergraduates at your university and randomly assign them
to one of three categories:
no journaling; journaling about what happened to them each week;
or journaling about what they're grateful for each week.
At the beginning and end of the study, you have participants fill out the
Beck Depression Inventory (BDI),
a 21-item pencil-and-paper questionnaire
that results in a score between 0 and 63,
with higher values representing worse depression.
You also measure other variables,
including gender, age, time spent socializing, and other coping mechanisms.


(i) Multinomial regression (baseline category logit model)
(ii) Linear regression
(iii) Logistic regression
(iv) Cox regression


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

ii

The outcome is not strictly continuous,
but it's nearly continuous.
Also, it's definitely not categorical, binary, or a time to event.

:::


### Part (c)

You are testing the efficacy of a variety of smoking cessation methods.
You recruit a large sample of people who are trying to quit smoking.
You measure several variables, including sex, age, age at first cigarette, etc.
You ask each participant when they last smoked,
and your outcome is the time until their next cigarette.


(i) Logistic regression
(ii) Multinomial regression (proportional odds model)
(iii) Cox regression
(iv) Multinomial regression (adjacent categories model)


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

iii

The outcome is time to an event, so Cox is the best option among those provided.

:::
